title: A critique of the over-politicization of CBT: A voice from the Global South
abstract: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) remains a premier evidence-based psychotherapeutic modality globally. However, decolonial and critical literature has increasingly sought to politicize the modality, dismissing it as a Western, hyper-rationalist, and reductionist framework that pathologizes structural trauma by locating systemic distress strictly within individual cognitive distortions. This paper presents a critical counter-perspective from the Global South, offering an immanent critique that challenges this adversarial academic narrative. Rather than treating CBT as a rigid instrument of neoliberal containment, we illustrate how its inherent structural flexibility, goal-focused blueprint, and pragmatic problem-solving stance actively dismantle learned helplessness, shifting vulnerable populations from passive sufferers to active creators of change. We examine how the core cognitive model harmonizes with culturally responsive practice in India, mapping modern individualistic aspirations alongside socio-centric identity networks-such as family hierarchies, religion, and caste-through contextual values clarification. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the synthesis of responsive validation and a directive clinical stance, both offered by CBTs, functions as an effective "parallel authoritative parenting" approach that mirrors care and discipline (or boundary-setting). In addition, core CBT concepts resonate with traditional Buddhist and Hindu concepts of the active observer rather than the passive recipient of environmental stimuli, as well as changing perspective to resolve cognitive deadlock. Hence, CBT presents robust clinical utility within India's rapidly expanding, educated, and tech-savvy urban populations. Finally, we address the paucity of regional research in the mainstream publication world and highlight how regional bodies, such as the Asian Cognitive Behavioural Therapies Association (ACBTA) and global bodies like the World Confederation of CBT (WCCBT), are helping local researchers transition from passive critique toward proactive structural interventions, including standardized cultural adaptation frameworks and showcasing these at global platforms. To summarize, this voice from the Global South argues that a dogmatic application of CBT is the real limitation, while its creative, innovative, mindful, scientifically rigorous evolution empowers Asian clinicians to deliver world-class, contextually grounded care.
